props.title: Z
props.initialSlug: Political thriller exposes Greek murder conspiracy

sections.content: **Z** (1969) revolutionized political thrillers with its white-knuckle examination of government corruption in Greece. Director Costa-Gavras crafted a searing indictment of the military junta through a fictionalized account of the real 1963 assassination of democratic politician Gregoris Lambrakis. The film's documentary-style approach, using handheld cameras and rapid editing, created a template for politically charged cinema that influenced works like **All the President's Men** (1976) and **Missing** (1982). Yves Montand's powerful performance as the doomed deputy and Jean-Louis Trintignant's determined investigator ground the film's mounting tension in human stakes.

sections.content: The film's influence on political cinema cannot be overstated. Its mix of thriller conventions with real political urgency inspired a wave of confrontational films about government corruption. **The Day of the Jackal** (1973) borrowed its procedural intensity, while **JFK** (1991) echoed its paranoid atmosphere and documentary techniques. The film's Oscar win for Best Foreign Language Film (a first for Greece) proved audiences would embrace challenging political content when wrapped in propulsive storytelling. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Political Thrillers

Z's DNA can be traced through later political thrillers that blend entertainment with activism. **Three Days of the Condor** (1975) adopted its theme of lone truth-seekers against systemic corruption. **The Official Story** (1985) used similar techniques to expose Argentina's Dirty War. More recently, **The Lives of Others** (2006) echoed Z's examination of state surveillance, while **No** (2012) borrowed its kinetic style to chronicle Chile's return to democracy.
